Donc dans le cas général, on peut aussi définir l'\uline{ordre} d'une fonction sur un diviseur premier $W$ : C'est l'entier associé à cette fonction dans le groupe des valeurs de l'anneau de valuation correspondant à $W$.

Le groupe abélien libre engendré par les diviseurs premiers de $V$ est appelé le groupe des \uline{diviseurs} de $V$. Chaque diviseur peut s'exprimer comme somme finie
\[
D=\sum n_iW_i
\]
où les $n_i$ sont des entiers $\ne 0$, et les $W_i$ sont des diviseurs premiers distincts. Le \uline{support} de $D$, i.e. l'ensemble des points dans les $W_i$, sera noté $|D|$.\margin{\uline{\unsure{$\sim W$}}} Si tous les $n_i$ sont $\geq 0$ on dira que $D$ est \uline{positif}. On voit qu'il y a une relation d'ordre partielle entre diviseurs.

Si $z$ est une fonction sur $V$, on peut lui associer le diviseur $\sum_W(\operatorname{ord}_Wz)W$, noté par $(z)$, la somme étant prise sur tous les diviseurs premiers. On sait que la fonction n'a qu'un nombre fini de zéros et de pôles, donc que cette somme est finie. Deux diviseurs $D_1$ et $D_2$ sont \uline{linéairement équivalents} s'ils diffèrent par le diviseur d'une fonction, i.e. s'il existe une fonction $z$ telle que $D_1=(z)+D_2$. Si $D$ est un diviseur, l'ensemble des diviseurs \uline{positifs} linéairement équivalents à $D$ sera noté par $\mathcal{L}(D)$. Il peut être vide. L'ensemble de tous les diviseurs linéairement équivalent à $D$ sera noté $\mathcal{L}^0(D)$.

statement: Ample classes are grouped by equality of positive integral multiples; the relation is positive rational proportionality, and high positive powers of an ample line bundle are very ample on a proper scheme over a field.
computation: Transitivity uses multiplication of the positive multipliers; positivity excludes opposite rays.
fate: The definition and elementary equivalence relation are standard; EGA II §§4.5–4.6, especially Proposition4.6.11, gives eventual very ampleness under the quasi-compact finite-type hypotheses; the proper-over-a-field case satisfies them. No novel integral primitive-class assertion is present. EGA II published1961, manuscript date not determined.

statement: For g:X→Y universally Stein with a section, the relative Picard sequence has kernel Pic(Y), and restriction to the section splits the Pic(Y) factor; the residual term is the pointed relative Picard functor.
computation: Rigidification at the section removes pullbacks from Y. Our proof-check P22 records the sheaf-level splitting and why it is not only a pointwise identity.
fate: FGA supplies the Picard-descent framework, and rigidification proves the exact sheaf-level splitting as checked in P22. \uline{Structure de certains groupes divisibles}.

\deleted{\unsure{Les}} Les groupes de torsion divisibles $\unsure{\mathfrak M|M}$ sont comme l'on sait isomorphes à des sommes directes de groupes $\mathbb Q_p/\mathbb Z_p$ ($p$ premiers); Ceux qui sont $p$-primaires sont donc isom. à des \deleted{sommes directes de} groupes $(\mathbb Q_p/\mathbb Z_p)^{(I)}$, où le cardinal de $I$ est bien déterminé; c'est aussi la dimension de l'espace vectoriel sur $\unsure{p}$ ${}_p\mathfrak M=\operatorname{Hom}(\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z,\mathfrak M)$.
\deleted{\unsure{Les $\mathfrak M$ en question} de torsion $p$-primaires sont d'ailleurs isomorphes}

Les conditions équivalentes

(i) $\mathfrak M$ groupe de torsion $p$-primaire, et ${}_p\mathfrak M$ est fini

(ii) $\mathfrak M$ isomorphe à un sous-groupe d'un $(\mathbb Q_p/\mathbb Z_p)^{\unsure{n}}$, \deleted{\unsure{$n\in\mathbb Z$}} $n$ entier $\geq0$.

(iii) $\mathfrak M$ isomorphe à un groupe $F+(\mathbb Q_p/\mathbb Z_p)^{\rho}$, où $F$ est un $p$-groupe de torsion fini, et $\rho$ un entier fini.
\margin{Modules sur un anneau de Dedekind.}
Sous ces conditions, $\rho$ est défini de façon unique [c'est aussi $\operatorname{rang}_{\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z}{}_p\mathfrak M^0$, où $\mathfrak M^0$ est le plus grand sous-groupe divisible de $\mathfrak M$] ainsi que la structure de $F$ [c'est $\mathfrak M/\mathfrak M^0$].

On peut de deux façons différentes faire correspondre à $\mathfrak M$ un module de type fini sur $\mathbb Z_p$:
On peut poser
\[
T_p(\mathfrak M)=\operatorname{Hom}(\mathfrak M,\mathbb Q_p/\mathbb Z_p)=\varprojlim_n\operatorname{Hom}({}_{p^n}\mathfrak M,\mathbb Q_p/\mathbb Z_p)
\]
\margin{$T_p$ \uline{foncteur} \uline{contravariant} en $M$}
[$\mathfrak M\mapsto T_p(\mathfrak M)$ établit une \inserted{anti-}équivalence de la catégorie des $\mathfrak M$ satisfaisant (i), et des modules de type fini sur $\mathbb Z_p$.

On peut prendre aussi
\[
T^p(M)=\varprojlim {}_{p^n}M
\]
\margin{$T^p$ foncteur \uline{covariant} en $M$}
où pour $m\geq n$, on envoie ${}_{p^m}M$ dans ${}_{p^n}M$ par $p^{m-n}$.

statement: A p-primary torsion abelian group with finite p-torsion is a finite p-group plus a finite direct sum of Prüfer groups. The statement concerns abstract groups, not finite flat group schemes.

Chevalley a vendu la démonstration suivante du \uline{lemme de Zariski}. Avec les notations du texte, on suppose $K,E,K(X),E(X)$ plongés dans un domaine universel U (algt. clos) ; soit $u=a(X)/b(X)$ dans $E(X)$, algébrique sur $K(X)$ ; il y a une infinité d'automorphismes s de U sur $K(X)$ ; les éléments $s(u)$ sont en nombre fini ; donc l'ensemble des s tels que $s(u)=u$ est un sous groupe d'indice fini du groupe des $K(X)$-automorphismes de U ; on en déduit que $a(X)=a^{\unsure{s|S}}(X)$ et $b(X)=b^{\unsure{s|S}}(X)$ pour les s de ce sous-groupe, si on a pris la précaution de supposer les polynômes a et b étrangers ; donc a et b ont leurs coefficients algébriques sur K, d'où etcétéra.

Il faut aussi montrer que si K est algébriquement fermé (ou quasi) dans E, et si K' est une extension algébrique finie de K, alors K' est algébriquement fermé (ou quasi) dans E(K'). Voici une démonstration valable en caract. 0, et qu'on pourrait essayer d'arranger : soit K'' la fermeture algébrique de K dans E(K') ; on a $K'\subset K''$ ; or $[E(K'):E]=$ $=[K':K]$ par disjonction linéaire ; de même $[E(K''):E]=[K'':K]$ comme $E(K'')=E(K')$, on en déduit $K''=K'$. C.Q.F.D.

Le $B$-module $E\otimes_A F$ est réunion des sous-modules $E'\otimes_A F$, $E'$ parcourant
l'ensemble des sous-modules de type fini de $E$. Si donc $\underline P$ appartient à
$\operatorname{Ass}_B(E\otimes_A F)$, il existe un $E'$ de type fini tel que $\underline P\in\operatorname{Ass}_B(E'\otimes_A F)$. D'après
(ii), il existe $\underline p\in\operatorname{Ass}_A(E')$ tel que $\underline P\in\operatorname{Ass}_B(F/\underline pF)$ ; comme
$\operatorname{Ass}_A(E')\subset\operatorname{Ass}_A(E)$, cela achève de démontrer la proposition.

COROLLAIRE.- \uline{Si} $A$ \uline{est noethérien}, \uline{et si} $\underline P\in\operatorname{Ass}_B(E\otimes_A F)$, \uline{on a}
$\pi^{-1}(\underline P)\in\operatorname{Ass}_A(E)$.

Cela résulte des propositions 1 et 2.

\uline{Remarques}.-

1) Supposons $A$ \uline{et} $B$ \uline{noethériens}. Soit $\underline P$ un idéal premier de $B$, et soit
$\underline p=\pi^{-1}(\underline P)$. Soit $S=A-\underline p$, et soit $k(\underline p)=S^{-1}(A/\underline p)$ le corps des fractions
de $A/\underline p$. Puisque $\underline P$ contient $\pi(\underline p)$, il définit un idéal premier de $B/\underline pB$, et
puisqu'il ne rencontre pas $S$, il définit aussi un idéal premier, noté $\underline{P'}$,
de $S^{-1}(B/\underline pB)=k(\underline p)\otimes_A B$. Alors, \uline{pour que} $\underline P\in\operatorname{Ass}_B(E\otimes_A F)$, \uline{il faut et il}
\uline{suffit que} $\underline p\in\operatorname{Ass}_A(E)$ \uline{et} $\underline{P'}\in\operatorname{Ass}_{k(\underline p)\otimes_A B}(k(\underline p)\otimes_A F)$.

Vu la prop.2, tout revient à voir que les conditions
\[
\text{`` }\underline P\in\operatorname{Ass}_B(F/\underline pF)\text{ ''}\quad\text{et}\quad
\text{`` }\underline{P'}\in\operatorname{Ass}_{k(\underline p)\otimes_A B}(k(\underline p)\otimes_A F)\text{ ''}
\]
sont équivalentes, ce qui résulte de la prop.5 du §1 (c'est ici que l'on
utilise l'hypothèse noethérienne sur $B$).

[D'après Grothendieck, l'énoncé ci-dessus est celui que l'on utilise dans
les schémas (le produit tensoriel par $k(\underline p)$ s'interprétant comme le passage
à la ``fibre au-dessus de $\underline p$ '').]

2) La proposition 2 s'applique notamment lorsque $B$ \uline{est plat sur} $A$ et que
l'on prend $F=B$. Le module $E\otimes_A F$ est alors simplement le module $E_{(B)}$
\uline{déduit de} $E$ \uline{par extension des scalaires}.

On recopie ensuite les deux dernières pages de l'Etat 1.

\begin{center}-:-:-:-\end{center}
\margin{21}

d'où $\operatorname{Ass}_B(F/\underline pF)\subset\operatorname{Ass}_B(E\otimes_A F)$, ce qui démontre l'inclusion $(\ast)$.

On va maintenant supposer que $A$ est \uline{noethérien}, et démontrer l'inclusion
opposée. On procèdera par étapes :

(i) $E$ \uline{est un module de type fini et} $\operatorname{Ass}_A(E)$ \uline{est réduit à un élément} $\underline p$.

D'après le th. 1 du §1, il existe une suite de composition $(E_i)_{0\leq i\leq n}$ de
$E$ telle que $E_i/E_{i+1}$ soit isomorphe à $A/\underline p_i$, où $\underline p_i$ est un idéal premier de $A$.
D'après le th.2 du §1, tous les $\underline p_i$ contiennent $\underline p$. Du fait que $F$ est $A$-plat,
les $E_i\otimes_A F$ forment une suite de composition de $E\otimes_A F$, et
$(E_i\otimes_A F)/(E_{i+1}\otimes_A F)$ s'identifie à $A/\underline p_i\otimes_A F=F/\underline p_iF$. En appliquant la
prop.3, on en déduit :
\[
\operatorname{Ass}_B(E\otimes_A F)\subset\bigcup\operatorname{Ass}_B(F/\underline p_iF).
\]

Soit donc $\underline P\in\operatorname{Ass}_B(E\otimes_A F)\cap\operatorname{Ass}_B(F/\underline p_iF)$. Si $\underline p_i\ne\underline p$, il existe $a\in\underline p_i$,
$a\notin\underline p$. D'après le cor.2 à la prop.2 du §1, l'homothétie de
rapport $a$ est injective dans $E$, donc celle de rapport $\pi(a)$ est injective
dans $E\otimes_A F$ ; mais d'autre part, $\pi(a)$ annule $F/\underline p_iF$, d'où $\pi(a)\in\underline P$, contradiction.
Ainsi $\underline p_i$ est nécessairement égal à $\underline p$, ce qui démontre la proposition dans le cas considéré.

(ii) $E$ \uline{est un module de type fini}.

Soient $\underline p_i$ les éléments de $\operatorname{Ass}_A(E)$, et soit $0=\bigcap Q_i$ une décomposition
primaire réduite correspondante (cf. §2, n°2). Le module $E$ se plonge dans
la somme directe des $E_i=E/Q_i$, et $E\otimes_A F$ se plonge dans la somme directe
des $E_i\otimes_A F$. On en déduit :
\[
\operatorname{Ass}_B(E\otimes_A F)\subset\bigcup\operatorname{Ass}_B(E_i\otimes_A F).
\]
D'après (i), on a $\operatorname{Ass}_B(E_i\otimes_A F)=\operatorname{Ass}_B(F/\underline p_iF)$, d'où la proposition dans
ce cas.

(iii) \uline{Cas général}.

\begin{center}
ALGEBRE COMMUTATIVE

CHAPITRE IV - DECOMPOSITION PRIMAIRE

\uline{Décomposition primaire et extension des scalaires} (Etat 2)

-:-:-
\end{center}
\margin{Rédaction n°355}

L'état 1 porte le n°352. Après l'avoir lu (et même avant), Grothendieck
a signalé au rédacteur qu'on pouvait généraliser le résultat principal, en
remplaçant l'un des anneaux par un module. La démonstration s'étend sans
changement, et c'est bien plus joli. Le rédacteur en a profité pour enlever
quelques hypothèses noethériennes inutiles.

\begin{center}-:-:-\end{center}

Dans tout ce qui suit, on désigne par $A$ et $B$ deux anneaux commutatifs,
et l'on considère un homomorphisme $\pi:A\longrightarrow B$. Cet homomorphisme fait de
$B$ une $A$-algèbre. On se donne en outre un $B$-module $F$ que l'on suppose \uline{plat}
\uline{sur} $A$.

PROPOSITION 1.- \uline{Soit} $\underline p$ \uline{un idéal premier de} $A$. \uline{Pour tout} $\underline P\in\operatorname{Ass}_B(F/\underline pF)$ \uline{on a}
$\pi^{-1}(\underline P)=\underline p$.

Puisque $\pi(\underline p)$ annule $F/\underline pF$, on a $\pi(\underline p)\subset\underline P$, d'où $\underline p\subset\pi^{-1}(\underline P)$. D'autre
part, si $a\in A-\underline p$, l'homothétie de rapport $a$ est injective dans $A/\underline p$, donc
aussi (puisque $F$ est $A$-plat) dans $F/\underline pF$, ce qui montre que $\pi(a)\notin\underline P$, CQFD.

PROPOSITION 2.- \uline{Soit} $E$ \uline{un} $A$-\uline{module}. \uline{On a} :
\[
(\ast)\qquad
\operatorname{Ass}_B(E\otimes_A F)\supset\bigcup_{\underline p\in\operatorname{Ass}_A(E)}\operatorname{Ass}_B(F/\underline pF)
\]
\uline{Lorsque} $A$ \uline{est noethérien}, \uline{l'inclusion} $(\ast)$ \uline{est une égalité}.

Soit $\underline p\in\operatorname{Ass}_A(E)$. Par définition de $\operatorname{Ass}_A(E)$, il existe une suite exacte :
\diagram{\begin{tikzcd}
0\arrow[r]&A/\underline p\arrow[r]&E.
\end{tikzcd}}

Puisque $F$ est plat sur $A$, on en déduit une suite exacte :
\diagram{\begin{tikzcd}
0\arrow[r]&F/\underline pF\arrow[r]&E\otimes_A F,
\end{tikzcd}}

1. \uline{Application des déterminants aux équations linéaires sur un corps commutatif.}

Les résultats des \S\S\ 5 et 6 donnent en particulier les suivants pour les
espaces vectoriels :

PROPOSITION 1.- \uline{Soit} $E$ \uline{un espace vectoriel sur un corps commutatif} ; \uline{pour que} $p$
\uline{vecteurs} $x_i$ ($1\leq i\leq p$) \uline{de} $E$ \uline{forment un système libre, il faut et il suffit que}
\[
x_1\wedge x_2\wedge\ldots\wedge x_p\ne0.
\]

C'est un cas particulier du \S6, n$^\circ$5, prop.7, tout élément $\ne0$ d'un corps étant
inversible.

COROLLAIRE 1.- \uline{Soit} $\underline X$ \uline{une matrice de type} $(m,n)$ \uline{sur un corps commutatif. Le rang
de} $\underline X$ \uline{est égal au plus grand des entiers} $p$ \uline{tels qu'il existe au moins un mineur
d'ordre} $p$ \uline{de} $\underline X$ \uline{qui ne soit pas nul.}

En effet, $\operatorname{rg}(\underline X)$ est le nombre maximum des colonnes de $\underline X$ linéairement indépendantes

l'expression des composantes d'un $p$-vecteur décomposable (\S6, n$^\circ$3, prop.5).

COROLLAIRE 2.- \uline{Pour qu'une matrice carrée sur un corps commutatif soit inversible,
il faut et il suffit que son déterminant ne soit pas nul.}

COROLLAIRE 3.- \uline{Pour qu'un système linéaire} homogène \uline{de} $n$ \uline{équations à} $n$ \uline{inconnues
sur un corps commutatif admette une solution non triviale, il faut et il suffit que
le déterminant de sa matrice soit nul.}

where $D$ is the group of divisors on $X$ concentrated on $X_o$ (which is a free group of finite type $\underline{Z}^{I}$, $I$ being the set of irreducible components of $X_o$). On the other hand, by the existence theorem for coherent sheaves, it is known that

statement: Let A be a complete noetherian local ring and f:X→Spec A a proper resolution, isomorphic over U=Spec A minus its closed point, with X regular and U schematically dense. Cartier divisors supported on X minus U give D→Pic(X)→Pic(U)→0; proper formal existence identifies Pic(X) with the compatible system of Pic(X_n). Only codimension-one exceptional components generate D; the blanket identification with every component of X_0 needs this qualification.
computation: Divisor restriction: extend a Cartier divisor from regular U by its codimension-one closure in regular X; its ambiguity is a divisor supported on X minus U. Formal existence applies to invertible sheaves and their inverses. See research/root_proofs.md §1.
fate: The divisor localization sequence is standard; formal existence is Grothendieck’s EGA III. The local-Picard application is developed explicitly by Lipman and Boutot. The two steps do not alone produce a representable quotient.

statement: A smooth proper pointed family over a connected locally noetherian base, with an abelian fibre, is expected to carry a unique abelian-scheme law. The pages prove uniqueness via rigidity, sketch the infinitesimal extension of multiplication, and explicitly leave the DVR closedness step to be developed. The opened published theorem is stated for a projective family; its proper analogue needs the corresponding algebraic-space extension theorem.
computation: For the first-order product deformation, H¹ of the product splits by Künneth, and the prescribed restrictions to the two identity axes determine both components; the H⁰ ambiguity is removed by the unit condition. This does not replace the DVR existence argument.
fate: The projective version is Mumford’s GIT Theorem6.14; Genestier–Ngô Theorem2.4.1 gives this statement and Proposition2.4.2/Lemma2.4.3 isolate the infinitesimal and DVR steps. These are exact matches for those steps. The broader proper scheme version was searched but is not certified here solely from the projective statement.

statement: The proposed characterization of torsion-dense smooth commutative groups by absence of additive factors is withdrawn: a nontrivial extension of an abelian variety by G_a in characteristic zero can still have Zariski-dense prime-to-characteristic torsion. For a nonzero vector-extension class by a one-dimensional vector group, the extension is anti-affine.
computation: For 0→G_a→G→A→0 in char0, [n] is an isomorphism on G_a and G[n]→A[n] is an isomorphism. If the closure of all torsion were proper, its connected quotient would be an additive quotient of an anti-affine group, impossible because every regular map to an affine scheme is constant. research/root_proofs.md §3.
fate: Brion’s classification of anti-affine groups supplies the later structural framework and includes characteristic-zero universal vector extensions. The source’s “no additive factor” necessity is explicitly rejected on the next sheet, not a surviving conjecture.

statement: For a commutative flat group scheme of finite presentation, multiplication by n invertible on the base is étale; without flatness its n-torsion is unramified under the stated finite-type conditions. The transcription’s possible “non comm.” cannot be retained: the nth-power map of a noncommutative group need not be unramified.
page_status_reason: Conditional refutation of the “noncommutative” reading; the commutative reading is correct.
computation: scripts/root_computations.py: noncommutative_power_counterexample. The conjugates [[1,−2u],[0,−1]] all square to I over k[u]; n=2 is invertible and GL₂ is smooth separated finite type. Thus every remaining hypothesis holds.
fate: The commutative statement is part of SGA3 and FGA236 Theorem2.5. If the ambiguous word really says noncommutative, GL₂ in characteristic zero supplies a counterexample: the involution diag(1,−1) has a positive-dimensional conjugacy class of square roots of1. The ink remains undecided.

statement: Finite étale closed subgroup schemes in a separated unramified group over a connected locally noetherian base that agree on one fibre agree everywhere; closed embeddings or the historical separated scheme convention are essential. For smooth commutative separated groups with finite étale prime-power torsion that is schematically dense, equality of rigid subgroups and of homomorphisms is detected on one fibre. Effective descent then holds for a faithfully flat finite-type cover with geometrically connected fibres, subject to the displayed rigidity hypotheses.
computation: Equality of finite étale closed subgroups is open and closed in the connected base, using the open unramified diagonal and its closedness from separation. A nonseparated étale double-origin trait has distinct sections agreeing generically, so separation cannot be omitted. Equality at all torsion levels plus schematic density forces equality of closed subgroups. Descent compares the two pullbacks on S′×_S S′ under the source’s connected-fibre hypotheses.
fate: SGA3 XI §6 gives the finite-level transporter and density mechanism with precise finiteness/flatness hypotheses. The primary-field-extension corollary is only sketched on the pages: spreading out a merely asserted rigid subgroup is not automatic from finite presentation.
fate_date: First circulation not independently dated; publication dates in the cited bibliography.
present_status: As of 2026-11-19: The finite-level rigidity theorem is established. The manuscript’s full primary-extension spreading assertion is retained as a qualified open step, not silently supplied by this proof.

statement: For proper flat finitely presented X/S, cohomologically flat in degree0 with geometric H⁰=k, a family B⊂Pic^τ_{X/S} of maximal abelian subvarieties yields an Albanese torsor under B∨, universal for maps to abelian torsors and compatible with base change. fate: Laurent–Schröer Theorem10.2 gives this precise criterion and construction; Theorem7.2 handles maximal abelian subvarieties under arbitrary field extension; Corollary10.5 gives the proper-field case with H⁰=k. statement: Smooth fibres alone do not make a relative Picard scheme smooth over a nonreduced base. In characteristic zero, for smooth projective X/S the identity component Pic⁰ is smooth even for nonreduced S; the full Picard scheme can still have jumping components that are not flat. Vanishing H²(O_{X_s}) gives a separate sufficient criterion for smoothness near s.
computation: The infinitesimal obstruction to extending a line bundle lies in H²(O)⊗I; its vanishing suffices. Constancy of h¹ in characteristic zero controls the identity component, not extension of every Néron–Severi class.
fate: Deligne’s Theorem5.5 proves cohomological local freeness and base change for smooth proper characteristic-zero families. Kleiman Remark5.21 applies it to Pic⁰, while Example5.22 exhibits the failure for the full Picard scheme, and Proposition5.19 proves the H² criterion. FGA236 Theorem3.5 also has a normal-fibre smoothness statement without reduced-base hypothesis.

statement: For a proper scheme over a field, numerical triviality of a line bundle equals τ-triviality; the geometric Néron–Severi group is finitely generated. In a proper finite-type family over a noetherian quasi-compact base, geometric NS ranks and torsion orders are uniformly bounded. Proper-surjective pullback, ample divisor restriction with fibre components dimension≥3, and [n] for n≠0 have the finiteness properties specified in the FGA addendum.

his_statement: (i) Let $X$, $Y$ be proper over $S$ neetherian, let $f:X\handwritten{\to}Y$ be a \uline{surjective} $S$ - morphism, assume for simplicity of the statement that the Picard preschemes exist, the\handwritten{n} $f:\underline{\mathrm{Pic}}_{Y/S}\handwritten{\longrightarrow}\underline{\mathrm{Pic}}_{X/S}$ is of finite type (and in fact affine if $S$ is the spectrum of a field), i. e.a subset $M$ of $\underline{\mathrm{Pic}}_{Y/S}$ is quasi-compact iff its image in $\underline{\mathrm{Pic}}_{X/S}$ is.
statement: A proper surjective morphism X′→X over a field induces an affine morphism Pic_X→Pic_{X′}; over an integral noetherian base it is generically representable by quasi-affine morphisms of finite type. The direction is contravariant. Affineness over a field and generic relative quasi-affineness are distinct assertions; finite type alone is weaker than either.
computation: Stein factorization and descent motivate the page’s proof sketch. The page135 arrow must be checked against pullback Pic(X)→Pic(X′); an arbitrary monomorphism of locally finite type groups is not automatically a closed immersion.
fate: Grothendieck’s conjecture in FGA232 Remark6.6 is proved in SGA6 XII, Raynaud written by Kleiman: Theorem1.1 gives generic relative representability and Corollary1.5 gives affineness over a field. The correspondence with the Murre letter is confirmed by Kleiman’s historical account, not inferred from a title.

his_statement: ``Problem A'' is the following: given $X/S$ and Module $F$ on $X$, to represent the functor on the category of $S$-preschemes taking any $S'/S$ into a one-element or into the empty set, occording as to whether $F'$ on $X'/S'$ is flat with respect to $S'$ or not, where $X'=X\mathbin{x}_{S}S'$, $F'=F\mathbin{x}_{S}S'$.
statement: For proper X→S with S locally noetherian and coherent F, the functor of base changes on which F becomes flat is represented by an unramified S-scheme locally of finite type. This is universal flattening, not merely a stratification whose members separately make F flat. The requested extension beyond the projective case is real and necessary.
computation: No numerical computation is asserted; mathematical qualification is stated in the claim.
fate: Murre’s May1965 Bourbaki exposé294, according to unpublished Grothendieck results, §3(A) Theorem2 and Corollary1 settles the proper case. ClassB records the checked publication under Murre’s authorship, while preserving its express attribution to Grothendieck. Stacks Lemma38.27.6 gives the current finite-presentation formulation. Without properness or purity, universal flattening can fail.

statement: An effective relative Cartier divisor is an invertible sheaf with a section that is a nonzerodivisor on each fibre, modulo multiplication by units. For proper flat X/S with universally f_*O_X=O_S and a cohomologically controlled sheaf L, the fibre of Div→Pic is the appropriate open part of the projectivized section module; for geometrically integral fibres every nonzero section is regular. Projective-bundle, local-freeness and base-change assertions require their separate hypotheses.

statement: For a cone over a smooth projective curve C with polarization L, formal neighbourhoods of the exceptional curve have successive Picard kernels H¹(C,L^n), n≥1, because H²(C,L^n)=0. statement: For a commutative locally algebraic group G over a field, its torsion-component subgroup is the inverse image of the torsion subgroup of π₀(G). Its union over exponent n is filtered by divisibility. If that locus is quasi-compact, only finitely many components occur and their torsion exponent is bounded. computation: A quasi-compact space mapping to a discrete étale component space has finite image. A finite set of torsion elements in an abelian group has a common annihilator, their least common multiple. This proves the bounded-exponent conclusion and explains the divisibility indexing.

statement: Let A be complete noetherian local, X=Spec A and X′ its puncture. If every component of X′ has dimension at least k+1 and X′ is connected in dimension at least k, then cutting by m≤k elements of the maximal ideal leaves every punctured component of dimension at least k−m+1 and connectedness in dimension at least k−m. In particular each such cut is connected. Finite avoidance and reduction to normality/S₂ occur in the proof, not as additional hypotheses of this final topological theorem.
computation: Induction on the number of cuts lowers both the relevant component-dimension bound and connectedness bound by one; the finite avoidance set ensures the depth condition on each cut. This is a proof-structure check, not a numerical experiment.
fate: The published SGA2 XIII Theorem2.1 and its local Bertini discussion develop this argument, using Hartshorne III3.6. The corrected inequality on58:13 points toward the required lower connectedness bound; an opposite inequality would reverse the induction.

Relative perfectness (for example smooth or suitable lci proper data) is needed to define determinant pushforward functorially. Translation acts trivially on NS(P^δ), so the resulting class φ(δ) descends independently of g.

statement: Let S have residue fields of characteristic zero and let G/S be a group scheme locally of finite presentation along the unit section e. Then G is smooth along e if and only if its conormal module ω_G/S=e*Ω_G/S is locally free. No prior flatness of G is added. This is the general group-scheme question on the page, distinct from the nearby Picard-specific smoothness question.
computation: Hypothesis-by-hypothesis comparison with the primary SGA3 VI B Proposition1.6. This is a targeted theorem check, not an independent proof of the EGA smoothness criterion.
fate: SGA3 VI B Proposition1.6 (Bertin) gives the exact equivalence, with local finite presentation along the unit stated explicitly. statement: Let f:X→S factor as X→Σ→S, with Σ→S finite and O_Σ→φ_*O_X an isomorphism preserved after every S-base change. Suppose g:Σ→X is a section of φ. Then Q(T)=Pic(X_T)/Pic(Σ_T) is the functor of g_T-rigidified line bundles up to isomorphism and is an fpqc sheaf. It identifies with the fppf-sheafified relative Picard functor of X/S, because line bundles on the finite scheme Σ_T become trivial Zariski locally on T. Flatness of Σ/S is not needed. The source’s successive Pic-prime and Pic-star conventions are preserved as historical stages, rather than identified without explanation.
computation: Normalize by L⊗φ_T*(g_T*L)^−1. Universal φ_*O=OΣ kills every rigidified automorphism, so fpqc descent is effective and unique. Over a local base, a finite algebra is semilocal and has trivial Picard group; a chosen line-bundle generator extends after shrinking. Thus Pic(Σ_T)/Pic(T) sheafifies to zero and the quotient Q agrees with Pic_{X/S}. No finite-flat hypothesis onΣ/S enters this proof. See root_proofs.md §5.
